canonical_truth.summary: An icejam-and-debris dam upstream of the brook crossing has been backing up meltwater for days. This morning a single deer hoof on a slipping stone is enough to release it. The brook surges briefly, runs brown with disturbed silt, and carries a season's worth of stranded debris past the bank — leaves, twigs, beetle-bearing sticks, a clutch of soaked beechnut shells from last fall's mast.
canonical_truth.location: upstream of the brook crossing, the bend just above the eddy
canonical_truth.concrete_outcome: The brook becomes briefly carrying. Anyone at the right stretch at the right minute gets exactly one chance at a moving forage. The surge leaves a fresh deer track in the new mud where the dam gave way.

perception_prompt.noticeable_surface: The brook is saying a different word this morning — fuller, faster, with brown water instead of gray, and small dark shapes traveling past faster than they should.

authorial_note.real_world_inspiration: Two US-flagged merchant vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz on 2026-05-04 — the first to cross since the start of Project Freedom — as the U.S. Navy reopened the waterway after a period of blockade.
authorial_note.translation_logic: A blocked waterway opens; things long-held pass through. For YY this becomes the icejam upstream giving way and a brief surge of carrying water, a moving forage one chance at a time. The geopolitical reopening becomes a sensory reopening — the brook's voice changes, and what had been stuck is suddenly moving.
authorial_note.restraint_reason: The world enters as water and small dark shapes traveling past — never as a concept of blockade or passage. YY does not understand strategic waterways; he understands that the brook is louder today and the things in it are running faster than they should.
